testing_objective: Determine whether the raw fields the Week 6 KPIs are built on are internally consistent
scenario: Recompute booking_lead_days from dates; recompute weekday from appointment_date; check duplicate IDs, negative lead times, previous_no_shows > previous_appointments, reminder_channel vs reminder_sent consistency
expected_result: Zero mismatches on all seven checks
actual_result: Zero mismatches on all seven checks (0/5,000 rows failed each)
issue_identified: None — successful validation, no issue invented
action_taken: None required; integrity confirmed and recorded as a reusable check

component_tested: Week 6 headline KPIs (no-show / attendance / cancellation rate)
testing_objective: Determine whether the published Week 6 KPI values reproduce from the raw data
scenario: Recompute the three rates from HealthConnect_Appointment_Data.csv and compare to the Week 6 report
issue_identified: No calculation error, but the denominator includes 263 cancellations, which are neither attendances nor no-shows
action_taken: Added a second, clearly labelled KPI pair on the decided-appointment base (51.15% / 48.85%) and labelled every dashboard panel with the base used
retest_result: Both KPI sets recompute correctly and are now explicitly distinguished

testing_objective: Determine whether the five published p-values and Cramér’s V values are correct and reproducible
scenario: Re-execute all five chi-square tests exactly as Week 6 coded them, then re-execute them against a binary Attended/No-Show outcome
expected_result: Week 6 values reproduce and the corrected test agrees with them
actual_result: All five reproduce to 4 d.p., confirming no coding slip. However the Week 6 tests were run against the 3-level appointment_outcome, so every Cramér’s V was divided by sqrt(2) and each test answered "is this feature associated with the 3-way outcome" rather than "with no-show". Corrected: lead time V 0.1967→0.2853, prior history 0.0889→0.1218, channel 0.0425→0.0562. appointment_type changed verdict: p=0.1042 (not significant) → p=0.0380 (significant)
issue_identified: HC-W7-01: chi-square tests run on a contaminated 3-level outcome. One published recommendation to the Data Science track ("Exclude — not statistically significant") rests on an invalid test
action_taken: Rebuilt all tests on the decided-appointment base with a binary outcome; applied Holm correction across the five-test family; reissued the artefact as HealthConnect_Week7_Feature_Relevance_v2.csv with a change_from_w6 column
retest_result: All five remain significant after Holm correction; relative ranking of lead time > prior history > channel ≈ reminder is unchanged, so the Week 6 prioritisation survives

component_tested: Week 6 recommendation #4 — "do not build appointment-type-specific policies"
testing_objective: Determine whether appointment_type should still be excluded once the test method is corrected
scenario: Likelihood-ratio test of a logistic model with appointment_type against the three-driver base model
expected_result: Unclear — the corrected chi-square (p=0.038) suggests the Week 6 exclusion may be wrong
actual_result: appointment_type is jointly significant (LR p=0.0325) but the practical gain is negligible: pseudo-R² rises only 0.0742→0.0755, and no individual type is significant (all level p>0.19)
pass_fail: FAIL — original rationale invalid, conclusion partially revised
issue_identified: HC-W7-02: Week 6 told Data Science appointment_type was "not statistically supported". That statement is false. The practical advice (deprioritise) happens to be reasonable, but for a different reason
action_taken: Reclassified appointment_type from "Exclude — not statistically significant" to "Optional / low priority — real but negligible", with the corrected evidence attached
retest_result: Revised classification holds under both the chi-square and LR tests

testing_objective: Determine whether the reminder effect is genuine or an artefact of lead-time confounding
scenario: Compare mean lead time by reminder status; compare unadjusted vs lead-time-adjusted odds ratios for reminder_binary
expected_result: If confounded, the reminder effect shrinks toward 1.0 once lead time is controlled
actual_result: Mean lead time is 29.7 vs 29.6 days (reminders are effectively randomly assigned w.r.t. lead time). Odds ratio 0.826 unadjusted vs 0.810 adjusted, p=0.0023 — the effect strengthens slightly rather than collapsing
issue_identified: None — the reminder finding survives the strongest available challenge
action_taken: Documented the confounding check as new supporting evidence; upgraded the confidence language on the reminder recommendation
retest_result: N/A — validation confirmed the existing conclusion
collaborating_track: Data Science (adjusted OR supplied as feature justification)

component_tested: Week 6 open item — reminder × prior-history interaction
testing_objective: Determine whether the unconfirmed interaction becomes significant on the corrected analysis base
scenario: Re-fit the logistic interaction model excluding cancellations
expected_result: Either the interaction becomes significant, or the Week 6 "do not engineer" caution is upheld
actual_result: Interaction p moves from 0.1432 to 0.1998 — further from significance
issue_identified: None new. The Week 6 decision to report this honestly rather than oversell it is vindicated
action_taken: Kept the "do not engineer" instruction in the v2 artefact; redrew the dashboard panel with hatching and an explicit "not a trend" label so the ascending bars cannot be misread
retest_result: Panel now states its own negative verdict; instruction to Data Science unchanged

component_tested: Week 6 headline conclusion — booking lead time is the strongest driver
testing_objective: Determine whether the lead-time conclusion holds inside every major patient segment or only in aggregate
scenario: Re-run the lead-time chi-square separately within each level of gender, appointment_type, reminder_sent and age_group (n≥100)
expected_result: The association holds in all segments if the finding is robust
actual_result: Significant in 14 of 15 segments (V range 0.21–0.32). The only failure is gender="Prefer not to say" (n=105, p=0.0587) — a power limitation, not a contradiction, since its effect size (V=0.29) is in line with the others
issue_identified: None material; small-segment power noted as a limitation
action_taken: Added the segment-stability evidence to the dashboard panel title so the claim is auditable

testing_objective: Determine whether each panel communicates its finding accurately and at the right level of confidence
scenario: Panel-by-panel review against the underlying data: are displayed statistics traceable to computation, are sample sizes visible, is uncertainty shown, can any panel be misread?
expected_result: Every panel is accurate and cannot be over-read
actual_result: Four defects. (a) All four panel titles hard-code statistics as literal strings, so they silently became wrong once the tests were corrected. (b) No sample sizes shown — the "2+ previous no-shows" bar (n=510) is drawn with the same visual weight as the n=2,745 bar. (c) No confidence intervals, so the reminder-channel ranking reads as settled when the intervals overlap heavily. (d) Panel 4 plots ascending bars of a pattern that was formally tested and found non-significant
issue_identified: HC-W7-03: dashboard annotations decoupled from computation; HC-W7-04: uncertainty and base sizes not communicated
action_taken: Rebuilt the dashboard: all titles now f-string interpolated from the live test results, Wilson 95% intervals on every bar, n labels on every category, a clinic-average reference line, the analysis base stated in the figure header, and panel 4 hatched and relabelled as descriptive-only
retest_result: Re-rendered; every displayed statistic now matches the computed value by construction and cannot drift again
collaborating_track: Project Management (dashboard is a shared decision artefact)
